teacher_guide.title: First, Next, Then, Last
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 2. First, Next, Then, Last — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students use the order words First, Next, Then, Last to put the steps of everyday tasks in order. Naming the order with these words is part of planning a sequence. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: cut the steps into cards so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Read the toast cards and label them First, Next, Then, Last together.
2. Do one together. Write the toast letters in order in the boxes.
3. Let them try. Students order the get-ready-for-recess cards on their own.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercises 1 & 2 — Make toast: First get the bread (B), Next put it in the toaster (D), Then push the lever down (A), Last take out the toast (C). Order: B, D, A, C.
Exercise 3 — Get ready for recess: First put on your coat (B), Next zip it up (A), Then put on your hat (D), Last go outside (C). Order: B, A, D, C.
Why the order matters: each step needs the one before — you zip after the coat is on, and toast comes out after it goes in.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: using the order words out of order. Point to each card and say its order word aloud.
Make it easier: lay the cards out and place the words First/Next/Then/Last beside them.
Make it harder: ask for a five-step task and which word fits the new middle step.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students put step-by-step instructions in the right order to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a set of steps, change or reorder one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child labels each step with the right order word and writes both tasks in order.
